1) Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) — fibrous cephalic plaque with overlying angiofibromatous papules; facial dome-shaped brown-red papules on nose/cheeks (classic facial angiofibromas/“adenoma sebaceum”); sacrococcygeal rubbery plaque compatible with a shagreen patch/collagenoma. No seizures or developmental delay does not exclude TSC. Next confirmatory steps: germline TSC1/TSC2 genetic testing (preferred), dermatopathology (punch biopsy of occipital plaque and a facial papule if genetic testing unavailable), and baseline screening imaging (brain MRI for cortical tubers/SEGA, renal ultrasound for angiomyolipomas).

2) Nevus sebaceus of scalp with secondary adnexal/neoplastic change (e.g., syringocystadenoma papilliferum, trichoblastoma) — explains an alopecic occipital plaque arising in early childhood with later development of discrete papules. Less able to explain the facial angiofibroma–type lesions and sacral plaque. Next steps: punch biopsy of the occipital plaque and representative papule; dermatologic surgical evaluation if neoplasm suspected.

3) Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) with plexiform/plaquelike neurofibroma on the occiput and multiple cutaneous neurofibromas on the face — can produce alopecia overlying a plaque and multiple papules on the face. Less likely given the described papule morphology and presence of a shagreen-like sacral plaque. Next steps: full skin exam for café-au-lait macules/axillary freckling, NF1 genetic testing if clinical suspicion, biopsy of a lesion (neurofibroma histology).

4) Isolated/connective tissue nevus (collagenoma) — the sacral plaque (shagreen) and occipital plaque could represent collagenous connective tissue nevi; occipital lesion could be a collagenoma producing focal alopecia. Facial papules might be a coexisting unrelated process. Next steps: punch biopsy of sacral and occipital plaques with dermatopathology (collagen content, elastic tissue studies).

5) Epidermal nevus syndrome / organoid epidermal nevus with extracutaneous findings — an epidermal nevus can present as a scalp plaque with secondary papules and alopecia and may be associated with other cutaneous plaques; CNS involvement can occur but is absent here. Next steps: biopsy of the plaque for epidermal nevus histology and targeted imaging/neurologic assessment if clinically indicated.

Rationale summary: The triad of a firm alopecic occipital plaque appearing in early childhood, multiple midfacial dome-shaped papules, and a sacrococcygeal rubbery plaque is most characteristic of TSC (fibrous cephalic plaque + facial angiofibromas + shagreen patch). To confirm, germline TSC1/TSC2 testing is the highest-yield investigation; if not available, targeted punch biopsies (occipital plaque and a facial papule) and dermatopathology support the diagnosis and help exclude nevus sebaceous or neurofibroma.
